header.title: Planning & Conducting a Statistical Investigation
header.subtitle: Pose a question · design a sample · collect · analyse · report with uncertainty

meta.lesson-focus: Plan and conduct a full sample-based investigation: pose a question, design the sample, collect data, analyse with appropriate summary statistics, report findings with acknowledgement of uncertainty; example contexts include pandemic-impact electricity data and reconciliation progress.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: plan and conduct statistical investigations involving samples of a population; use ethical and fair methods to make inferences about the population and report findings, acknowledging uncertainty
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: Valid inferences about populations can be made by drawing conclusions from representative samples

html.section0_intro: Three quick questions from earlier work. They warm up the statistics skills you’ll use today.
html.section_warmup:
A real investigation that is secretly today’s statistics.

During the 2020 pandemic lockdowns, many people stayed home all day. Energy companies wanted to know: did households use more electricity than before?

There are hundreds of thousands of households in South Australia. Measuring every single one would cost too much and take too long, so researchers studied a carefully chosen sample instead.

From a sample of just a few hundred households, statisticians estimated the change for the whole population — then reported it honestly as an estimate with uncertainty, not an exact fact. Today you will plan and run your own investigation the same way: pose a question → design a sample → collect → analyse → report.
html.vocab_cards:
Population
Tap to flip
The whole group you want to draw a conclusion about.
Example: every household in South Australia.
Census
Tap to flip
Collecting data from every member of the population — a complete count.
Example: the national Census counts every resident.
Sample
Tap to flip
A smaller group chosen from the population that you actually collect data from.
Example: 500 households chosen from all SA households.
Random sample
Tap to flip
A sample where every member has an equal chance of being chosen — this helps avoid bias.
Example: numbering every student and drawing names at random.
Inference
Tap to flip
A conclusion about the whole population drawn from sample data — it always carries some uncertainty.
Example: “use rose by about 4 kWh/day” estimated from a sample.

html.worked_example:
Investigation: Did households use more electricity during the 2020 lockdown than in 2019?

1
Pose the question & design the sample
The population is all SA households. Measuring every one is impractical, so we take a random sample of 10 households and record the increase in daily electricity use (kWh) from 2019 to 2020. Choosing them randomly keeps the sample fair and representative.
Population: all SA households  •  Sample: 10 randomly chosen households  •  Variable: increase in daily use (kWh)
2
Collect & organise the data
Here is the increase in daily use (kWh) for the 10 sampled households, sorted smallest to largest:
2,  3,  3,  4,  4,  4,  5,  5,  6,  8
3
Analyse with summary statistics, then report
Plot the data and summarise it. Mean = 44 ÷ 10 = 4.4 kWh; median = (4 + 4) ÷ 2 = 4 kWh; mode = 4 kWh; range = 8 − 2 = 6 kWh.
Report (acknowledging uncertainty)On average, sampled households increased daily use by about 4.4 kWh. Because this comes from a sample of only 10, the true population figure may differ — a larger sample would make the estimate more reliable.
html.we_do_intro: Reconciliation Australia runs a national survey, the Australian Reconciliation Barometer, to measure progress in the relationship between First Nations (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander) peoples and non-Indigenous Australians. A school cannot survey all 900 of its students, so it takes a random sample of 8 students and asks each to rate, from 1 to 10, how well they understand the histories and cultures of First Nations Australians. Sample ratings: 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9. Let’s analyse it together.
html.strategy_section:
PRACTICE CORE
Order the steps
Put each investigation into the correct sequence, then press Check order.

🧩Order the investigation steps

Each investigation below has its five stages jumbled. Use the ▲ and ▼ buttons to put them in order — pose → design the sample → collect → analyse → report — then press Check order. Correct cards turn green and lock.

Scenario 1 — Did SA households use more electricity during the 2020 lockdown?
  • Record each sampled household’s daily electricity use for 2019 and 2020.
  • Ask: did households use more electricity during the 2020 lockdown than in 2019?
  • Conclude that use rose by about 4 kWh/day on average, noting the estimate carries uncertainty.
  • Randomly select 500 households from all SA households to keep the study manageable.
  • Find the mean increase and draw a dot plot of the differences.
Scenario 2 — Testing a factory’s light globes (a census would destroy the stock).
  • Because testing every globe destroys it, randomly select 60 globes to test.
  • Calculate the mean and median burn-time of the 60 sampled globes.
  • Ask: what is the mean burn-time of the globes this factory makes?
  • Estimate the mean burn-time for all globes, acknowledging the sample may not be exact.
  • Burn each of the 60 sampled globes and record how many hours each one lasts.
Scenario 3 — Has students’ understanding of First Nations histories and cultures grown over the year?
  • Compare the mean survey scores and the spread between the start and end of the year.
  • Randomly select 50 students from across all year levels so the sample is representative.
  • Report whether understanding appears to have improved, acknowledging the uncertainty of a sample.
  • Ask: has students’ understanding of First Nations histories and cultures grown over the year?
  • Survey the same 50 students with the same questions at the start and end of the year.

retrieval.q: Find the mean of this small sample: 4, 6, 6, 8, 11.
retrieval.hint: Add all five values (35), then divide by how many there are (5).
The values are already in order — the median is the middle one.

retrieval.q: A group surveys 50 of the 1200 students at a school. The 50 students are the sample; the 1200 students are the … Type population or sample.
retrieval.hint: The population is the whole group you want a conclusion about.

matchTerms.html: Decide what to find out and identify the population
Choose a fair, random method to select who to survey
Record measurements or responses from the sample
Work out the mean, median and range and draw a plot
State a conclusion about the population, noting the uncertainty

weDo.q: How many students are in this sample?
Find the mean rating of the sample.
weDo.hint: Add the eight ratings (56), then divide by 8.

weDo.q: The whole school has 900 students. Can we say the mean rating of ALL 900 is exactly 7? Type A (yes, exactly) or B (no — 7 is an estimate that carries uncertainty).
weDo.hint: A sample gives an estimate of the population, not its exact value.

checkpoint.q:
Put the investigation stages in order. Using the letters, type them in the correct sequence separated by commas (e.g. B,D,A,E,C):
A Collect data • B Pose the question • C Report findings • D Design the sample • E Analyse the data.
checkpoint.hint: What must you decide first, before collecting anything? What comes last?

checkpoint.q: A sample is representative when it: A) is as large as the whole population, B) has characteristics similar to the population, C) only includes people who volunteer. Type A, B or C.
checkpoint.hint: Representative means the sample looks like the population in miniature.

practice1.q: Find the mean of this sample: 5, 7, 7, 9, 12.

practice1.hint: Already in order — take the middle value.
The mode is the value that appears most often.

practice1.q: You want the average daily electricity use of all 700 000 SA households. Should you take a census or a sample? Type census or sample.
practice1.hint: A census of 700 000 households would cost far too much and take too long.

practice1.q: A survey selects 300 people from a city of 50 000. The 50 000 people are the … Type population or sample.
practice1.hint: The whole city is the group we want a conclusion about.

practice1.q:
Type the 5 stages in the correct order using letters (e.g. B,E,D,A,C):
A Analyse • B Pose the question • C Report • D Collect data • E Design the sample.
practice1.hint: Pose, then design the sample, then collect, then analyse, then report.

practice1.q: A sample of 6 households recorded these weekly recycling amounts (kg): 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 6. Find the mean.

Which sampling method is the most fair and least biased? A) ask only your friends, B) number every student and use a random number generator, C) ask the first 10 people who arrive early. Type A, B or C.
practice1.hint: A fair method gives every member of the population an equal chance.

practice1.q: A sample mean is 4.4 kWh. The best way to report this about the population is: A) ‘Every household increased by exactly 4.4 kWh’, B) ‘Household use increased by about 4.4 kWh on average, though the true value may differ’, C) ‘No household changed’. Type A, B or C.
practice1.hint: Report a sample result as an estimate, acknowledging uncertainty.

practice2.q: Find the median of this sample (even count): 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 14.
Sample of 10 households, increases in kWh: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 10. The value 10 is much larger than the rest. Which is less affected by this outlier — mean or median? Type mean or median.
practice2.hint: An outlier pulls the mean toward it, but barely moves the middle value.

practice2.q: For that same data (1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 10), find the median.
A researcher samples 250 people from 5000 customers. What percentage of the population is sampled? Type just the number of percent.
True or false: increasing the sample size generally makes an inference about the population more reliable. Type true or false.
practice2.hint: Larger samples usually reduce the uncertainty of the estimate.

practice3.q: A council samples 8 households’ quarterly electricity bills ($): 210, 240, 240, 260, 275, 290, 300, 425. Find the median bill (in dollars).
practice3.hint: They are in order; average the 4th and 5th values: (260 + 275) ÷ 2.

practice3.q: For the same 8 bills (210, 240, 240, 260, 275, 290, 300, 425), find the mean bill (in dollars).
practice3.hint: Sum is 2240; divide by 8. Notice the mean is above the median — the $425 bill is an outlier.

practice3.q: A school of 800 students runs the reconciliation attitudes survey on a random sample of 40 students. 28 of the 40 agree that ‘learning First Nations histories is important’. Using the sample proportion, estimate how many of all 800 students would agree.

A group surveys only their own friendship circle about a school-wide question. Their inference is likely to be: A) unbiased and representative, B) biased because the sample is not representative, C) certain and exact. Type A, B or C.
practice3.hint: A friendship circle is not chosen randomly, so it may not reflect the whole school.

exitProbs.q:
Type the 5 stages of a statistical investigation in order using letters (e.g. C,E,B,D,A):
A Report findings • B Collect data • C Pose the question • D Analyse • E Design the sample.
exitProbs.hint: Pose, design the sample, collect, analyse, then report.

exitProbs.q: Why do we acknowledge uncertainty when reporting a sample result? A) because samples are always wrong, B) because a sample is only part of the population, so it gives an estimate, C) because maths is hard. Type A, B or C.
exitProbs.hint: A sample gives an estimate of the population, not an exact certainty.

exitProbs.q: In one or two sentences, explain why a random sample is fairer than surveying only your friends when investigating a school-wide question.
exitProbs.hint: Think about who gets a chance to be included, and whether your friends represent the whole school.
